articles.summary: India's next renewable energy milestone will not just be about how much clean power it can generate. It will be about how reliably it can deliver it. At the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit & Expo 2026, Sumant Sinha, Founder, Chairman & CEO, ReNew, joined Shipra Malhotra, Editor - Special Initiatives (ETCIO and ETCISO), The Economic Times Business Verticals, for a conversation on the next phase of India's energy transition. Sinha identifies three priorities that will determine the pace of progress: Scaling energy storage: A combination of battery storage and pumped hydro will be essential to address the mismatch between daytime renewable generation and evening power demand. Strengthening transmission infrastructure: Expanding grid capacity is critical to ensuring that growing renewable generation can reach consumers. Building domestic clean-tech supply chains: India needs capabilities across solar modules, batteries, rare earth permanent magnets and the components that underpin these technologies. The conversation also explores the growing electricity requirements of data centres, the potential of green molecules, corporate renewable procurement and India's opportunity to emerge as an alternative manufacturing destination in the global clean-tech supply chain. One clear takeaway: India's energy transition is increasingly an infrastructure, manufacturing and energy-security challenge, not just a generation target. Watch the full conversation.

articles.summary: What will it take to build a more diversified global solar supply chain? China’s manufacturing capacity is now twice global demand, reshaping global markets and making supply chain diversification an energy security priority. India has an opportunity to emerge as a competitive second source. Realising it will require manufacturing scale, cost competitiveness, access to capital and policies that reward supply chain resilience. Importing countries also have a role to play. Diversification requires recognising the strategic value of alternative sources, not just evaluating procurement on price. At ReNew, we operate 6.5 GW of module and 2.5 GW of cell capacity, with ingots and wafers next. The next phase of the solar transition must be about diversifying not just energy sources, but also where the technology is manufactured. From my conversation on The New Industrialists. articles.summary: ReNew calls for responsible, community-focused data centres in India, prioritising zero water, clean energy, and domestic manufacturing expansion, says Vaishali Nigam Sinha ReNew Energy Global Plc, a leading decarbonisation solutions company, has recently announced a major expansion of its clean energy and manufacturing footprint in Andhra Pradesh, with a focus on data centre infrastructure, backward integration in solar manufacturing and rare-earth permanent magnet production. Company’s Co-Founder and Chairperson (Sustainability) Vaishali Nigam Sinha is excited particularly about entering the rapidly evolving data centre landscape, but at the same time aware of the duty to comply with the relevant ESG (Environmental, Social and Governance) framework. Speaking to The Hindu on the sidelines of an industry event at the CII Partnership Summit-2026, Ms. Sinha said that ReNew was supplying a substantial portion of its clean energy to data centres, and it factored in ‘responsible governance’ as critical to the sector's expansion. She emphasised that India needs ‘responsible data centres’ that care for the communities in which they operate and give back to them, by trying to embed zero water, zero noise, and clean energy technologies to the extent possible. “The country really needs data centres because the Fourth Industrial Revolution is not going to wait for us,” she observed. She said that ReNew was in the process of integrating its supply chain upwards in the renewables sector (integrating ingots, silicon and polysilicon). She said that ReNew was in the process of integrating its supply chain upwards in the renewables sector (integrating ingots, silicon and polysilicon). Air-cooling systems On public and regulatory concerns surrounding water consumption by large data centres, ReNew CEO Sanjay Varghese said air-cooling systems must be the way forward as they help reduce water requirements by half or more. Though air-cooling is relatively expensive, it accounts for a small fraction of the huge capital expenditure being incurred on data centres, he noted, suggesting that desalination should be undertaken as a long-term solution along with air cooling, especially in water-sensitive areas. Renewable energy Ms. Sinha described the renewable energy sector's current hurdles, such as securing land, talent, and faster execution, as ‘good problems’ driven by rapid growth and constructive public-policy engagement. She said ReNew laid greater focus on domestic R&D and equipment manufacturing to achieve the much-needed self-reliance, as though raw materials were available globally, refining capacity and capital equipment manufacturing were heavily concentrated in China. Mr. Varghese stated that ReNew was now producing solar modules and cells and setting up ingot and wafer manufacturing. The next phase involves backward integration into high-purity polysilicon made from domestically available quartz to eliminate import dependence. He pointed out that ReNew has recently won a government tender to manufacture rare-earth permanent magnets, an indispensable part of electric mobility.
